Cell Injury and Death

Hasan Samra, MD • Week 6: Foundations of Immunology • Lecture 7 • Cellular Pathology • Enriched Study Guide

What this lecture is really trying to teach

This lecture is the pathology framework for what happens when stress exceeds a cell's ability to maintain homeostasis. Mild or brief injury can remain reversible; severe or prolonged injury crosses into irreversible mitochondrial/membrane failure, cell death, and recognizable necrosis patterns.

  • Mechanism: ATP depletion, pump failure, calcium accumulation, ROS, membrane injury, and organelle damage.
  • Reversible injury: cellular/organelle swelling, ribosome detachment, hydropic change, and fatty change.
  • Irreversible injury: severe mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane damage, lysosomal leakage, and necrosis.
  • Nuclear sequence: pyknosis -> karyorrhexis -> karyolysis.
  • Five patterns: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid.
  • Board enrichment: ROS/reperfusion injury, the point of no return, necrosis vs apoptosis, and classic vignette associations.
Need to memorize - master list
  1. Main injury targets: mitochondria, membranes, cytoskeleton, DNA, protein synthesis.
  2. Hypoxia -> ↓ oxidative phosphorylation -> ↓ ATP -> Na+/K+ pump failure -> Na+/water influx + K+ efflux -> swelling.
  3. Low ATP also drives glycolysis -> glycogen depletion + lactic acidosis and ribosome detachment -> ↓ protein synthesis.
  4. High intracellular Ca2+ activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, ATPases.
  5. Reversible injury: RER swelling/ribosome loss, swollen mitochondria with preserved cristae, hydropic/fatty change.
  6. Irreversible injury: severe mitochondrial swelling/cristae destruction, membrane damage, lysosomal leakage.
  7. Nuclear death sequence: pyknosis -> karyorrhexis -> karyolysis.
  8. Necrotic cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic/pink.
  9. Coagulative: ischemia in solid organs except brain.
  10. Liquefactive: brain infarct + bacterial abscess.
  11. Caseous: tuberculosis.
  12. Fat: pancreatitis + saponification.
  13. Fibrinoid: vasculitis + malignant hypertension.

  1. Understand the basic molecular aspects of cellular injury.
  2. Focus on the role of hypoxia in cellular injury.
  3. Recognize differences between reversible and irreversible injury using homeostasis, ultrastructure, and light microscopy.
  4. Recognize nuclear and cytoplasmic light-microscopy changes after cell death.

Need to memorize - calcium injury

Phospholipases damage membranes • proteases damage proteins/cytoskeleton • endonucleases damage DNA • ATPases worsen ATP depletion.

⭐ BOARD ENRICHMENT - ROS

Recognize superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical. ROS cause lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation/cross-linking, and DNA damage. Major defenses include superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and antioxidant vitamins.

LO 2 - Hypoxia and Ischemic Injury

Hypoxia: inadequate oxygen availability to cells.
Ischemia: inadequate tissue perfusion/blood flow; Samra illustrates arterial obstruction.
⭐ BOARD ENRICHMENT - HYPOXIA vs ISCHEMIA

Ischemia is generally more damaging because impaired blood flow reduces oxygen and substrates such as glucose while limiting waste removal.

1
O2 fallsOxidative phosphorylation decreases.
→
2
ATP fallsEnergy-dependent pumps fail.
→
3
Na+ accumulatesWater follows -> swelling.
→
4
Glycolysis risesGlycogen falls; lactate/pH worsen.
→
5
Ribosomes detachProtein synthesis decreases.
Need to memorize - hypoxic injury

↓O2 -> ↓ATP -> pump failure + swelling + anaerobic glycolysis -> glycogen depletion + lactic acidosis + ↓protein synthesis.

⭐ BOARD ENRICHMENT - ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION

Restoring blood flow can produce an additional burst of injury through ROS generation, Ca2+ overload, mitochondrial injury, and inflammatory-cell recruitment. Reperfusion can save viable tissue while simultaneously injuring borderline cells.

LO 3 - Reversible vs Irreversible Injury

Reversible injury: injury from which a cell can recover if the stressor is removed before permanent membrane/mitochondrial failure.
LevelReversible findingsMeaning
Biochemical↓ATP, ↓pH, ↓glycogen, ↓protein synthesisEnergy stress
IonicNa+, Ca2+, water influx; K+ effluxLoss of ion/volume homeostasis
EMRER swelling + ribosome detachment; mitochondrial swelling with preserved cristaeOrganelle injury still compatible with recovery
Light microscopyCloudy swelling, vacuoles, hydropic degeneration, fatty changeVisible reversible morphology
Lecture p. 11. Hydropic swelling: pale swollen hepatocytes compared with nearby more-normal cells.
Hydropic degeneration: water accumulation caused by failed ion-pump/osmotic control.
Fatty change: intracellular lipid accumulation, classically in liver; Samra illustrates excessive alcohol use.
⭐ BOARD ENRICHMENT - THE POINT OF NO RETURN

The most useful threshold is persistent inability to restore mitochondrial ATP generation plus severe membrane dysfunction. Extensive plasma, mitochondrial, and lysosomal membrane damage makes recovery impossible.

Irreversible injury: severe/prolonged injury producing unrecoverable mitochondrial and membrane damage and cell death.
  • Severe mitochondrial swelling with cristae destruction.
  • Extensive plasma-membrane damage.
  • Severe lysosomal swelling/rupture -> hydrolase leakage.
  • Digestion of cellular and nuclear components.
  • Intracellular proteins leak into blood.
🩺 CLINICAL TRANSLATION

Samra's example is troponin: myocardial necrosis disrupts membrane integrity, allowing intracellular proteins to enter blood and become diagnostic biomarkers.

FeatureReversibleIrreversible / necrotic
MitochondriaSwollen, cristae preservedSeverely swollen; cristae destroyed / function unrecoverable
MembraneIon dysfunction/blebbing can occurMajor loss of integrity and leakage
LysosomesNo catastrophic ruptureHydrolases leak -> autodigestion
NucleusNo necrotic sequencePyknosis -> karyorrhexis -> karyolysis
OutcomeCan recoverCell dies

LO 4 - Morphology of Cell Death

Need to memorize - nuclear sequence

Pyknosis -> karyorrhexis -> karyolysis. Shrink -> fragment -> dissolve.

TermMeaningMemory hook
PyknosisShrinkage and chromatin condensationPacks down
KaryorrhexisNuclear fragmentationBreaks apart
KaryolysisNuclear fading/dissolutionLysis = disappears
Lecture p. 18. Pyknotic nuclei become small and dark.
Lecture p. 19. Karyorrhexis fragments nuclei; karyolysis fades/dissolves them.
Eosinophilia: increased pink H&E staining. Necrotic cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic because proteins denature and basophilic RNA is lost.
Need to memorize - dead cell on H&E

More pink cytoplasm + shrinking/fragmenting/fading nucleus.

LO 5 - Five Patterns of Necrosis

The comparison table to know cold

PatternMorphology/mechanismClassic settingFast clue
CoagulativeProtein denaturation > enzymatic digestion; architecture preserved earlyIschemia in solid organs except brainGhost outlines
LiquefactiveEnzymatic digestion dominates; architecture dissolvesBrain infarct; bacterial abscessLiquid/pus/cavity
CaseousAmorphous debris, architecture lostTuberculosisCheese-like granuloma center
FatLipase injury + Ca2+ soap formationAcute pancreatitisChalky saponification
FibrinoidFibrin/plasma proteins in damaged vessel wallVasculitis; malignant hypertensionBright pink vessel wall

1. Coagulative necrosis

Coagulative necrosis: architecture remains recognizable because denaturation outpaces proteolytic digestion.

Classic with ischemic injury to heart, kidney, liver, spleen, and most other solid organs. Brain is the exception.

Lecture p. 26. Necrotic myocardium remains structurally recognizable while inflammatory cells enter.
Need to memorize

Solid-organ infarct -> coagulative, except brain.

2. Liquefactive necrosis

Liquefactive necrosis: hydrolytic digestion dominates, rapidly dissolving tissue into liquid/semi-liquid debris.

Classic in brain ischemia and bacterial abscesses rich in neutrophil enzymes.

Lecture p. 32. Brain liquefactive necrosis with dissolution of normal architecture.
MEMORY HOOK

Brain and bacteria become broth.

3. Caseous necrosis

Caseous necrosis: amorphous granular proteinaceous debris with loss of normal architecture and a gross cheese-like appearance.

Samra's key association is tuberculosis; board context commonly places it within a granuloma.

Lecture p. 36. Tuberculous caseation replaces normal tissue with amorphous debris.
Need to memorize

TB -> caseous -> cheese-like granuloma center.

4. Enzymatic fat necrosis

Fat necrosis: adipocyte destruction by lipases, classically during pancreatitis.
1
Pancreatic enzymes escapeLipases reach surrounding fat.
→
2

→
3
SaponificationFatty acids bind Ca2+.
→
4
Chalky depositsCalcium soaps form.
Lecture p. 39. Pancreatic fat necrosis with a labeled region of saponification.
Need to memorize

Pancreatitis -> lipase -> fatty acids -> Ca2+ soaps -> chalky saponification.

5. Fibrinoid necrosis

Fibrinoid necrosis: necrotic vascular-wall injury containing intensely eosinophilic fibrin/plasma-protein material.

Think vasculitis and malignant hypertension.

Lecture p. 42. Bright eosinophilic vessel-wall injury in vasculitis.
Need to memorize

Fibrinoid = vessel wall.

Board Add-On - Necrosis vs Apoptosis

⭐ EXTERNAL BOARD ENRICHMENT - NOT A PRIMARY SAMRA OBJECTIVE
NecrosisApoptosis
Usually pathologic severe injuryPhysiologic or pathologic programmed death
Cell/organelle swellingCell shrinkage
Membrane ruptureMembrane remains relatively contained; apoptotic bodies form
Contents leak -> inflammationContents packaged for phagocytosis -> little inflammation

Intrinsic pathway: mitochondrial stress -> BAX/BAK-mediated cytochrome-c release -> caspase-9 -> executioner caspases; BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibit this pathway.

Extrinsic pathway: death-receptor signaling (for example Fas-family signaling) -> caspase-8 -> executioner caspases.

Board Add-On - Gangrenous Necrosis

⭐ COMMON BOARD TERM - NOT ONE OF SAMRA'S FIVE

Gangrene is a clinical/gross descriptor rather than a unique microscopic pattern. Dry gangrene generally reflects coagulative ischemic necrosis of an extremity; superimposed infection and liquefaction produce wet gangrene.

Common Exam Traps

TrapCorrect logic
Hypoxia = ischemiaIschemia is perfusion failure and usually causes broader metabolic deprivation.
Cell swelling means deathSwelling is a classic early reversible change.
Any mitochondrial swelling is irreversibleReversible injury can show swelling with preserved cristae.
Karyolysis occurs firstPyknosis -> karyorrhexis -> karyolysis.
All infarcts are coagulativeBrain infarction is the liquefactive exception.
Liquefactive only occurs in brainAlso abscesses/infections.
Any granuloma = caseousCaseation is classically TB; not all granulomas caseate.
Fibrinoid = infarcted myocardiumThink vessel wall: vasculitis/malignant hypertension.

What to Memorize vs Understand

Tier 1 - memorize cold

ATP-depletion chain; Ca2+ enzymes; reversible vs irreversible morphology; nuclear sequence; five necrosis patterns + classic associations.

Tier 2 - understand deeply

Why pump failure causes swelling; why mitochondrial/membrane failure becomes irreversible; why denaturation vs digestion creates different necrosis morphology.

Tier 3 - external board enrichment

ROS defenses, reperfusion injury, necrosis vs apoptosis, intrinsic/extrinsic apoptosis, gangrene terminology.

Tier 4 - lower priority

Memorizing every exact histology image. Prioritize pattern recognition + mechanism + clinical setting.

FUN MEMORY SET

Coagulative = contours stay • Liquefactive = liquid • Caseous = cheese • Fat = fatty acids grab calcium • Fibrinoid = fibrin in vessel walls.

30-second end-of-lecture summary

Cell injury begins when stress disrupts ATP production and homeostasis. Hypoxia lowers oxidative phosphorylation and ATP, causing pump failure, swelling, glycolysis, acidosis, calcium accumulation, and reduced protein synthesis. Early organelle swelling is reversible, but severe persistent mitochondrial and membrane dysfunction becomes irreversible, causing lysosomal leakage, nuclear destruction, membrane rupture, and necrosis. Necrotic nuclei progress from pyknosis to karyorrhexis to karyolysis, while cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic. The five patterns are coagulative (solid-organ ischemia except brain), liquefactive (brain infarct/abscess), caseous (TB), fat (pancreatitis/saponification), and fibrinoid (vasculitis/malignant hypertension).
